power.title: Power Analysis Check
report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

We left out 1 file that software creates by itself, not the authors: operating system (1). They hold nothing a reader can use, but they clutter the repository, and software can mistake them for real files (for example a `._` copy of a `.csv` for data).

*Remove these:* *Operating system* files: macOS adds a `__MACOSX` folder and a `._` copy of every file it puts in a zip, and `.DS_Store` files to folders; Windows adds `Thumbs.db` and `desktop.ini`. On a Mac, create zips from the command line with `zip -r -X`, or remove them afterwards with `zip -d archive.zip "__MACOSX/*" "*.DS_Store"`. *RStudio session files* (`.Rproj.user/`) hold open tabs and unsaved edits; *R history* (`.Rhistory`) lists the commands typed in a session and can hold file paths and passwords; *Jupyter checkpoints* (`.ipynb_checkpoints/`) are automatic copies of notebooks; *compiled Python files* (`__pycache__/`, `.pyc`) are recreated when the code runs; *open-document lock files* (`~$...docx`, `.~lock...#`) are left while a document is open; *editor backups* (`file~`, `.bak`, `.swp`) and *temporary files* (`.tmp`, `.temp`) are copies a program made by itself.

*Keep only on purpose:* *version control* folders (`.git`, `.svn`, `.hg`) hold the project's history, which can include earlier versions of files and data that was later removed; *editor settings* (`.idea`, `.vscode`) can hold paths on your own computer. Internet addiction has become a prominent mental health and behavioral addiction risk in the digital age.
Although using the Internet itself-for social media, shopping, gaming, and work etc.

-is not inherently problematic, and users can generally obtain immediate pleasure and emotional relief, they are also prone to developing patterns of uncontrolled, repetitive, and continued use despite known harm (Shi et al., 2022).

text.text: Existing research has consistently shown that Internet addiction is closely associated with negative emotions such as depression and deficits in cognitive control (A et al., 2026; Ioannidis et al., 2019; Wang et al., 2026).

text.text: The Interaction of Person-Affect-Cognition-Execution model (I-PACE) proposes that negative emotions, as distal predisposing factors, can drive Internet addiction through interactions among the cognitive-affective-executive systems, while cognitive control may serve as a "brake" that buffers this pathway (Brand et al., 2019; 2025).

text.text: Survey studies have found that cognitive control significantly moderates the relationship between Internet addiction and negative emotional states (Bai et al., 2026), but the neural mechanisms underlying this association remain unclear.

text.text: Brain functional changes provide an important window for understanding how cognitive control moderates the depression-Internet addiction link.
Internet addiction can be conceptualized as an imbalance between the dual pathways of "feels better" and "must do" and the "stop now" cognitive control process (Brand, 2022a).

text.text: Depressive mood may drive Internet addiction through the "feels better" pathway and temporarily alleviate depressive mood; after repeated use, the behavior gradually becomes habitualized and progressively shifts toward the "must do" pathway, manifesting as continued use despite known harm.
"Stop now" involves cognitive control and subserves functions such as inhibiting impulses and maintaining goal-directed behavior (Brand, 2022a).

text.text: At the neural level, this imbalance mainly involves the prefrontal-striatal circuit, with regions such as the dorsolateral prefrontal cortex participating in cognitive control and regions such as the dorsal and ventral striatum participating in reward processing and habit formation (Brand et al., 2016).

text.text: In recent years, advances in resting-state fMRI and brain functional connectivity network research have provided testable network-level evidence for the aforementioned "dual-pathway-cognitive control" imbalance.

An activation likelihood estimation (ALE) meta-analysis of cognitive control tasks showed consistent hyperactivation in the left middle frontal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule in individuals with Internet addiction, suggesting that "stop now" is not simply hypoactivation of the control network but may instead reflect compensatory over-recruitment when the frontoparietal control network is inefficient (Li et al., 2026).

text.text: Using a publicly available fMRI dataset employing a cognitive control task (Liu et al., 2026), this study intends to characterize the roles of cognitive control-related brain regions and networks in the depression-Internet addiction relationship, employing region-of-interest selection and task-modulated functional connectivity methods to examine individual brain regions and brain networks, respectively.

text.text: We propose the following hypothesis: task-modulated functional connectivity between regions involved in the frontoparietal control network and the subcortical reward network carries the moderating effect of cognitive control on the link between depression and Internet addiction; specifically, the stronger the functional connectivity, the stronger the moderating effect of cognitive control on the link, manifesting as a weaker or even nonsignificant depression-Internet addiction association; the weaker the functional connectivity, the weaker the moderating effect of cognitive control, manifesting as a stronger depression-Internet addiction association.

text.text: This study used behavioral and functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data from the publicly available database (Liu et al., 2026).

The original data collection obtained ethics approval and informed consent, as described in the original dataset publication.
The original study initially enrolled 38 participants (10 males; mean age = 19.88 years, SD = 1.67, age range = 17-24 years).
None of the participants had been previously diagnosed with psychiatric or neurological disorders.

After data quality screening, four participants were excluded due to excessive head motion (translation > 3 mm or rotation > 3°) or poor MRI data quality, leaving a final sample of 34 participants for analysis.

text.text: The present study aimed to investigate the potential mechanisms by which cognitive control contributes to the association between Internet addiction and depressive states.
Therefore, only the experimental materials directly relevant to the present research question were selected from the public database and included in subsequent analyses.

Specifically, these comprised the runs under the no-social-distraction condition of the global-local attention allocation task, the Internet Addiction Test (IAT), and the Beck Depression Inventory (BDI).

The global-local attention allocation task is commonly used to examine individual differences in attentional resource allocation and has been applied in previous studies (Medaglia et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2024).
text.formatted: The global-local attention allocation task is commonly used to examine individual differences in attentional resource allocation and has been applied in previous studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b27">(Medaglia et al., 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Wei et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: This paradigm includes both congruent and incongruent trials and can therefore be used to assess cognitive control processes.
The stimuli were hierarchical compound figures consisting of a larger global shape and a smaller local shape, with shape types including circle, X, triangle, and square.
In congruent trials, the global and local shapes were identical; in incongruent trials, they differed.
The two trial types each accounted for 50% of trials and were presented randomly.

Participants were required to make judgments based on stimulus color: if the figure was green, they reported the shape of the larger figure; if it was white, they reported the shape of the smaller figure.

The response mapping was as follows:1 = square,2 = circle,3 = triangle, and4 = X. Each stimulus was presented for 2000 ms on a black background, with an inter-trial interval (ISI) of 1500-4500 ms (mean = 3000 ms).

Because the present analysis focused on general cognitive control rather than social information interference effects, not all three conditions from the original study-online social distraction, online non-social distraction, and baseline-were included.

The present study selected only the global and local attentional levels under the baseline condition, as well as the congruent and incongruent trial types, to exclude interference from irrelevant factors such as social information.
Conditions of social distraction, non-social distraction, and baseline corresponded to different runs, and the run order was counterbalanced across participants.
In each run, a working memory control task and the global-local attention task were administered alternately to control for potential confounding variables.
Therefore, only the fMRI run corresponding to the baseline condition was analyzed in this study.
The baseline run comprised 48 trials in an event-related design, with 24 trials for the global condition and 24 trials for the local condition.
Visual stimuli were presented using E-Prime 3.0 software (Psychology Software Tools, Pittsburgh, PA, USA) on a HP computer with a screen resolution of 1920 × 1080 and a refresh rate of 60 Hz.
The Internet Addiction Test was used to measure the severity of individuals' internet addiction (Young, 1998).

text.text: The scale consists of 20 items (Sample item: "How often do you find that you stay online longer than you intended?").
Items are rated on a 5-point Likert scale (1 = rarely,5 = always).
A higher total score indicates a stronger tendency toward internet addiction.
The Beck Depression Inventory was used to assess the presence and severity of depressive symptoms in adolescents and adults (Beck, 1961).

text.text: The scale consists of 21 items rated on a 4-point scale.
A higher total score indicates more severe depressive symptoms.
Behavioral data were analyzed using general linear models (GLMs).

Specifically, the total score of IAT was treated as the dependent variable, with age and gender as covariates, while the total score of BDI and the mean reaction times and accuracy rates under the six conditions of the global-local attention allocation task (global congruent, global incongruent, local congruent, local incongruent, global incongruent -global congruent, and local incongruent -local congruent) were treated as independent variables.
The main effects and interaction effects of each predictor were examined.
For conditions with significant interaction effects, simple effects analyses were further conducted to clarify the specific patterns of effects across conditions.
Whole-brain images were acquired in an MRI environment using a 3T Prisma MRI scanner (Siemens, Erlangen, Germany) equipped with a 64-channel head-neck coil.

Task-related functional images were obtained using a magnetization-prepared rapid gradient-echo sequence, with the following main scanning parameters: repetition time (TR) = 2000 ms, echo time (TE) = 30 ms, field of view (FOV) = 224 × 224 mm, voxel size = 2 × 2 × 2.3 mm, 62 slices, slice thickness = 2 mm, flip angle = 90°, and multi-band factor = 2.

To exclude participants with obvious brain lesions and to improve the standardization of functional imaging data, T1-weighted high-resolution anatomical images were acquired using a spoiled gradient-echo pulse sequence with the following parameters: TR = 2530 ms, TE = 2.98 ms, matrix size = 224 × 256, voxel size = 0.5 × 0.5 × 1 mm, 192 slices, slice thickness = 1 mm, flip angle = 7°, and multi-band factor = 2.
First-level GLM analyses were performed using SPM12.
The model included regressors for global congruent, global incongruent, local congruent, and local incongruent trials.
To improve motion control, six head motion parameters were included as covariates.

Based on previous studies (Beckes et al., 2021; Ford et al., 2011; Ito et al., 2008; Kahn & Shohamy, 2013; Krienen & Buckner, 2009), MNI coordinates for the DLPFC, VMPFC, DMPFC, caudate nucleus, putamen, nucleus accumbens, substantia nigra, and ventral tegmental area were selected to define ROIs with a radius of 6 mm (Figure 1).

To further examine the moderating effects of functional connectivity across different brain regions on the relationship between negative affect and internet addiction, we performed task-modulated functional connectivity analyses using the Task-Modulated Functional Connectivity (TMFC) toolbox (https://github.com/Masharipov/TMFC_toolbox) (Masharipov et al., 2024).

text.text: The Brainnetome Atlas (BNA; 246 regions) was adopted as the ROI parcellation scheme.

This atlas comprises 210 cortical regions and 36 subcortical regions, each classified according to the Yeo 17-network system (including visual peripheral/central, somatomotor A/B, dorsal attention A/B, salience/ventral attention A/B, limbic A/B, control A/B/C, default A/B/C/D, and subcortical) (Yeo et al., 2011).

text.text: Regions not assigned to any Yeo network (36 subcortical regions in total) were collectively assigned to the "subcortical network" (Subcort), yielding 18 networks in total: 17 Yeo cortical networks plus 1 subcortical network.
The 246 ROIs were imported into the TMFC toolbox to construct the ROI set.

Task-based functional connectivity was estimated using beta-series correlation based on BSC-LSS approach. (1) least-squares separate (LSS) GLMs: this method estimates a beta value separately for each trial via LSS regression, thereby yielding a trial-wise neural activity time series.
For each participant, each condition, and each trial, a separate GLM was fitted.
The target trial was represented by its own regressor, all remaining trials of the same condition were collapsed into a single regressor, and other conditions were left unchanged.
In this way, one beta image was generated for each trial.
(2) BSC-LSS functional connectivity estimation: for each ROI, the first eigenvariate was extracted from the beta values of all voxels within that region to form the ROI's beta series.
Pearson correlation coefficients were then computed between the beta series of any two ROIs and converted to Fisher's Z values, yielding a 246 × 246 ROI-to-ROI functional connectivity matrix.

Linear contrasts were used to generate between-condition differences in functional connectivity, including (i) global incongruent -global congruent and (ii) local incongruent -local congruent conditions.

To improve the biological interpretability of the functional networks, the 246 × 246 ROI-level connectivity matrix was reduced to the network level based on the 17 Yeo cortical networks plus 1 subcortical region.

Because the present study primarily focused on functional connectivity patterns between cortical regions and subcortical regions, only connections between cortical networks and the subcortical region were analyzed.
For each pair of networks, the connectivity strength was averaged across all ROI pairs, yielding 17 network-level connectivity variables that served as moderators in subsequent moderation analyses.
GLMs were used to test whether network-level functional connectivity moderated the relationship between IAT total scores and BDI total scores.

The dependent variable (Y) was the IAT total score; the independent variable (X) was the BDI total score; the moderator (W) was functional connectivity under each condition contrast; and covariates included age and sex.

All first-level GLM analyses were performed in SPM12; BSC-LSS functional connectivity analyses were conducted using the TMFC toolbox; ROI-level beta extraction and moderation analyses were implemented in MATLAB R2025b using custom scripts.

Because this study involved a focused, hypothesis-driven analysis that reduced the number of multiple comparisons, an uncorrected significance level of p < 0.05 was adopted, and effect sizes (partial η² and R²) were also reported to evaluate the robustness of the results.

Discussion This study aimed to investigate the behavioral and neural evidence for underlying mechanisms by which cognitive control modulates Internet addiction and depression.

At the behavioral level, individuals' accuracy under conflict conditions significantly moderated the relationship between Internet addiction and depression; enhanced cognitive control attenuated the positive association between Internet addiction and depression.
At the neural level, some prefrontal regions and some subcortical regions showed antagonistic moderating effects on the association between Internet addiction and depression.

Specifically, increased activation in some prefrontal regions attenuated the positive association between Internet addiction and depression, whereas increased activation in some subcortical regions strengthened this positive association.

Brain network results provided convergent evidence, showing that increased functional connectivity between the control network and the subcortical network attenuated the positive association between Internet addiction and depression.

The present study found that enhanced cognitive control attenuates the positive association between Internet addiction and depression, as reflected in the finding that accuracy under conflict conditions significantly moderated the relationship between Internet addiction and depression.
This is consistent with previous findings (Bai et al., 2026).
text.formatted: This is consistent with previous findings <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Bai et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Compensatory Internet use theory suggests that individuals tend to turn to online activities to alleviate stress and negative emotions in real life (Kardefelt-Winther, 2014).

For individuals with weaker cognitive control, however, it is more difficult to inhibit the affect-driven drive to engage in online activities when such use gets more habitual via repeated Internet use (Brand et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For individuals with weaker cognitive control, however, it is more difficult to inhibit the affect-driven drive to engage in online activities when such use gets more habitual via repeated Internet use <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Brand et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: It may also result in weaker actual and perceived competence of emotional regulation, further prompting individuals to engage in compensatory Internet use, thereby strengthening the link between depression and Internet addiction.
At the neural level, our results of activation in different brain areas also corroborated the behavioral findings.

Specifically, some prefrontal regions, including the left DLPFC and left VMPFC, negatively moderated the positive association between Internet addiction and depression, such that the positive association was weaker in individuals with stronger activation in these regions.

Previous studies have found that the DLPFC and VMPFC are responsible for cognitive control functions (He et al., 2021; MacDonald et al., 2000), integrating somatic markers or value signals related to emotional experience into decision-making and exerting self-control over tempting behaviors (Bechara, 2005).
text.formatted: Previous studies have found that the DLPFC and VMPFC are responsible for cognitive control functions <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(He et al., 2021;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">MacDonald et al., 2000)</ref>, integrating somatic markers or value signals related to emotional experience into decision-making and exerting self-control over tempting behaviors <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Bechara, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: Therefore, individuals with stronger DLPFC and VMPFC activation are better able to integrate value signals and implement control behaviors.

In subcortical regions, including the substantia nigra, nucleus accumbens, and caudate nucleus, their activation positively moderated the positive association between Internet addiction and depression, such that the positive association was stronger in individuals with stronger activation in these regions.
This helps to explain the "feels better" and "must do" pathways in individuals with Internet addiction, which may indirectly attenuate the role of cognitive control.

The substantia nigra amplifies craving and activates both the "feels better" and "must do" pathways (Zhang et al., 2016); the nucleus accumbens enhances reward-seeking and use motivation (Cai et al., 2016); and the caudate nucleus promotes behavioral automatization, gradually decoupling use behavior from reward-provided motivation (Niu et al., 2024).

text.text: Collectively, these processes contribute to dysregulated cognitive control and strengthen the association between depressive mood and Internet addiction.

Based on the brain atlas and the TMFC method, this study further found that the functional connectivity pattern between a subregion of the frontoparietal control network and the subcortical brain network negatively moderated the positive association between depression and Internet addiction; when the functional connectivity between the two was stronger, the positive association between Internet addiction and depression was weaker.

This supports the argument at the level of task-based dynamic brain networks, namely that the cognitive control "stop now" module located in the frontoparietal region regulates the subcortical "feels better" and "must do" pathways (Brand, 2022b).

text.text: The frontoparietal control network includes the lateral prefrontal cortex, anterior cingulate cortex, and inferior parietal lobule (Yeo et al., 2011), and supports processes such as flexible and adaptive cognitive control (Vincent et al., 2008), whereas subcortical regions are responsible for functions such as reward, motivation, and craving (Cai et al., 2016; Niu et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2016).

text.text: The observed moderating effects of frontoparietal-subcortical functional connectivity on the depression-Internet addiction association provide additional neural evidence that stronger connectivity reflects stronger cognitive control inhibition of the bidirectional depression-Internet addiction link, whereas weaker connectivity reflects weaker inhibition.

This supports an interactive rather than purely unidirectional top-down regulatory account (Cruz et al., 2023), which corresponds to the early-and late-stage model of I-PACE (Brand et al., 2019; 2025).
text.formatted: This supports an interactive rather than purely unidirectional top-down regulatory account <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">(Cruz et al., 2023)</ref>, which corresponds to the early-and late-stage model of I-PACE <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">(Brand et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2025)</ref>.

text.text: In the early stage, Internet use is more goal-directed (e.g., for emotional relief) because of reward sensitivity; at this time, top-down regulation dominates and cortical regions such as the frontoparietal control network mainly assume decision-making roles, determining when to start and stop Internet use.

In the late stage, individuals' behavioral patterns have become more automatized; subcortical structures are simultaneously positioned at both early (sensory input) and late (motor output) stages in whole-brain circuits, meaning that they have a major influence on originally goal-directed behavior.

This processing mode for Internet stimuli and the final output of use behavior can bias decision-making in cortical regions such as the frontoparietal control network in a bottom-up manner, thereby preventing fully effective top-down decisions and leading to habitual behavior.
This view is also supported by relevant literature (Zhu et al., 2025).
text.formatted: This view is also supported by relevant literature <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Zhu et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: This study has the following limitations.
First, it did not use longitudinal data, making it difficult to directly verify the causal relationships of functional connectivity patterns.
Second, the study was conducted in a laboratory environment, and brain functional patterns in real-world Internet use contexts remain to be further explored.
Third, depression and Internet addiction were assessed using self-report scales; future studies should incorporate more objective behavioral measures to verify the robustness of the findings.
Overall, at the behavioral level, this study found that cognitive control negatively moderates the positive relationship between Internet addiction and depression.

Based on neuroimaging data, it further found that functional connectivity patterns between regions involved in the frontoparietal control network and subcortical regions such as the striatum negatively moderate the positive relationship between Internet addiction and depression.

The present study thereby verifies that the cognitive control "stop now" module regulates the imbalance in the subcortical "feels better" and "must do" pathways, and further validated the I-PACE theoretical model at the level of brain imaging.
These findings may help inform future neurofeedback treatment for individuals with Internet addiction and the design of specific therapeutic targets.
